specPoints.text: explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer, such as insulation

primer.text: Most wasted energy escapes by heating, so cutting waste means cutting conduction and convection. This note assembles the toolkit — low-conductivity insulators, immobilised fluids, thickness — and applies it where houses need it: fibreglass in the loft and insulation in the cavity walls.

lessons.title: Reducing unwanted energy transfers
lessons.opening: Wasted energy mostly leaves by heating, so the fight against waste is a fight against conduction and convection. Low-conductivity materials block the first, preventing fluid movement blocks the second, and insulation — loft fibreglass, cavity wall fill — applies both ideas where a house loses most.
keyPoints: Energy dissipated to the surroundings is the main source of wasted energy transfers.
Conduction is reduced by using materials with low thermal conductivity — insulators.
Convection is reduced by preventing the fluid that forms the currents from moving.
An insulator’s effectiveness depends on its thermal conductivity (lower is better), its density (more dense conducts more) and its thickness (thicker insulates better).
Loft insulation (fibreglass) and cavity wall insulation lower a house’s rate of cooling.

low.restatement: Stop conduction with poor conductors, stop convection by immobilising the fluid, and buy thickness: insulation is those three rules applied to lofts and wall cavities.
low.analogy: Dressing for snow: a thick coat of low-conductivity fabric with still air trapped inside is a wearable insulation panel.
low.examPointer: The three effectiveness factors — conductivity, density, thickness — with their directions (lower, lower, higher) are the examinable list.

medium.restatement: Houses lose energy fastest where large warm surfaces meet moving cold air; fibreglass lofts trap still air above, and cavity wall fill turns the gap between two wall layers into a low-conductivity barrier.
medium.analogy: Two doors against the draught: the loft lid closes the top exit, the cavity fill plugs the wall’s hollow middle.
medium.examPointer: Link insulation to money and emissions when asked why: less wasted energy means lower bills and fewer greenhouse gases from the saved heating.

check.stem: What is the main source of wasted energy transfers?

options.text: energy transferred electrically
options.explanation: Electrical transfer is often the useful route.

options.text: energy dissipated to the surroundings
options.explanation: Dissipation to the surroundings is the main waste source.

options.text: energy stored in the thermal store
options.explanation: Stored energy is not yet wasted.

options.text: energy transferred by radiation only
options.explanation: Radiation is one dissipation route, not the whole account.

check.stem: How is energy transfer by conduction reduced?

options.text: by using materials with low thermal conductivity
options.explanation: Insulators conduct heat poorly.

options.text: by using metals wherever possible
options.explanation: Metals are the best conductors.

options.text: by making the fluid move faster
options.explanation: That describes convection, and faster movement transfers more.

options.text: by thinning the insulating layer
options.explanation: Thinner insulates worse.

check.stem: How is energy transfer by convection reduced?

options.text: by preventing the fluid that forms the currents from moving
options.explanation: No movement means no convection current.

options.text: by increasing the thermal conductivity of the fluid
options.explanation: Conductivity is the conduction route.

options.text: by heating the fluid more strongly
options.explanation: Stronger heating drives stronger currents.

options.text: by using a denser fluid
options.explanation: Density alone does not stop the current.

check.stem: Which insulator property list and directions is correct?

options.text: low conductivity, high density, thin layer
options.explanation: High density conducts more and thin insulates worse.

options.text: low conductivity, low density, thick layer
options.explanation: Lower conductivity, lower density and greater thickness all insulate better.

options.text: high conductivity, low density, thick layer
options.explanation: High conductivity is the conductor’s trait.

options.text: only thickness matters
options.explanation: All three factors matter.

check.stem: Why does the air trapped between fibreglass fibres make it a good insulator?

options.text: the air conducts heat quickly out of the house
options.explanation: Trapped air conducts poorly.

options.text: trapped air cannot move to form convection currents, and as a gas it conducts very slowly
options.explanation: Both failure modes of transfer are blocked.

options.text: the glass fibres reflect all radiation
options.explanation: The mechanism is the trapped air, not reflection.

options.text: the fibres absorb the heat permanently
options.explanation: Nothing absorbs and destroys energy.

check.stem: State what cavity wall insulation fills.
check.modelAnswer: The gaps or cavities between the external walls of a house.

check.stem: State the material often used for loft insulation and the property that makes it work.
check.modelAnswer: Fibreglass (glass fibre); air held between its fibres cannot move, which makes it a strong insulator.

check.stem: Explain why a denser insulating material conducts more than a less dense one.
check.modelAnswer: Denser insulators pack particles nearer together, so the collision chain hands energy on faster; less dense materials leave bigger gaps and slow the chain.

check.stem: A house has uninsulated loft and unfilled wall cavities. State two changes that lower its rate of cooling and name the transfer route each one mainly blocks.
check.modelAnswer: Lay fibreglass loft insulation, which mainly blocks conduction (with trapped air also stopping convection), and fill the wall cavities with insulation, which blocks conduction through the walls and prevents convection currents forming in the cavity.

glossary.definition: A material with low thermal conductivity that reduces energy transfer by conduction.
Insulating material filling the gap between a house’s external wall layers.
A reinforced plastic of woven material and glass fibres; trapped air between the fibres makes it a good insulator.
How quickly a object transfers energy to its surroundings; insulation lowers it.

figures.caption: Insulated mugs are used to maintain the temperature of hot or cold drinks
Less energy is transferred by conduction and convection if the cavity is insulated
